A disjunction is a separation or disconnect — a gap between two things that don't fit together, or that pull in different directions.

Think of the word in pieces: "dis-" means apart, and "junction" means a joining point. So a disjunction is the opposite of a junction — it's where things fail to connect, or come apart.
The word is used in two broad ways: one in everyday language, and one in logic and philosophy.
Meaning 1 — Everyday Use: A Gap or Mismatch

In everyday English, a disjunction refers to a noticeable gap, inconsistency, or lack of harmony between two things that are supposed to be connected, aligned, or consistent with each other.

Examples:

  • "There is a clear disjunction between the government's promises and its actions."
    — What was promised and what was actually done are misaligned. They don't match.
  • "She noticed a disjunction between how he behaved at work and how he behaved at home."
    — Two sides of the same person feel disconnected, like they don't belong to the same story.
  • "The film suffers from a disjunction between its slow pace and its action-heavy plot."
    — The style and the content are working against each other.

The key feeling this meaning captures is: "These two things should go together, but they don't." There's a break, a fault line, a mismatch.
Meaning 2 — Logic and Philosophy: An "Or" Statement

In logic, a disjunction has a precise, technical meaning. It is a compound statement that combines two claims using the word "or."

For example:

"It is raining or it is sunny."

This whole sentence — both parts joined by "or" — is the disjunction. Each individual part ("It is raining" and "It is sunny") is called a disjunct. So a disjunction always has at least two disjuncts.

Why does this matter?

In logic, a disjunction is considered true as long as at least one of its disjuncts is true. It is only false when both disjuncts are false.

Disjunct ADisjunct BIs the Disjunction True?
  • If A is true and B is false → the disjunction is true
  • If A is false and B is true → the disjunction is true
  • If both A and B are true → the disjunction is true
  • If both A and B are false → the disjunction is false

The Two Types of Disjunction in Logic

There is an important distinction here that logicians care about:

1. Inclusive disjunction ("or, possibly both")
This is the standard, default meaning of "or" in logic. It allows for the possibility that both options are true at the same time.

"You can have cake or ice cream."
(In the inclusive sense, you could have both.)

In symbolic logic, this is written as A ∨ B, and read as "A or B."

2. Exclusive disjunction ("either...or, but not both")
This is a stricter version. Here, the statement is only true when exactly one of the two disjuncts is true — but not both.

"The switch is either on or off."
(It cannot be both at the same time.)

In symbolic logic, this is written as A ⊕ B, and is sometimes called "XOR" (exclusive or).

In everyday speech, when someone says "either...or," they often mean the exclusive version. But in formal logic, unless stated otherwise, "or" is typically treated as inclusive.
How the Two Meanings Are Related

They're more connected than they might seem. Both meanings share the same underlying idea of two things being separated or in tension:

  • In everyday use, a disjunction is a separation between things that don't align (a mismatch, a gap).
  • In logic, a disjunction is a statement that presents two separate possibilities (an "or" claim).

In both cases, the word points to two distinct things existing apart from each other — whether it's two contradictory realities, or two separate propositions.

UseWhat it means

In everyday language, a disjunction is a gap, break, or mismatch between two things that should fit together but don't.

In logic, a disjunction is a compound statement joining two claims with "or." It is true if at least one of the claims is true. An inclusive disjunction allows both to be true; an exclusive disjunction requires exactly one to be true.
A Few More Examples in Context

• "There's a troubling disjunction between the school's stated values and how it treats its students." — A gap between words and reality.
  • "Philosophers often debate the disjunction between the mind and the body." — The idea that the mind and body are fundamentally separate.
  • "The logical disjunction 'The train is late or the schedule is wrong' is true so long as at least one of those is actually the case." — A classic logical usage.
  • "He experienced a sense of disjunction when he returned home after years abroad — familiar places felt foreign." — A feeling of internal disconnect.

That's the complete picture of "disjunction" — from its common use to its precise technical role in logic.
